items.title: 13.10.2 Reaction with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide

source_refs.note: Topic 13.10.2 with Quick Check 13.5, printed pages 300-301.

blocks.text: When chlorine reacts with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide (NaOH), it forms sodium chloride (NaCl) and sodium chlorate (V) (NaClO₃). It is another example of disproportionation reaction.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book's equation is not balanced (6 Cl and 6 Na on the left, 2 of each on the right). The balanced equation is 3Cl₂(g) + 6NaOH(aq) → 5NaCl(aq) + NaClO₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l): five Cl atoms are reduced to -1 and one is oxidised to +5.
Chlorine is oxidized from 0 to +5 in NaClO₃. Chlorine is reduced from 0 to -1 in NaCl
This disproportionation reaction shows how the temperature of the reaction influences the products formed, demonstrating the versatility of chlorine in undergoing redox reactions.

blocks.prompt: a) How would KI react with conc. H₂SO₄. What does this reaction indicate about the reducing power of iodide?
blocks.explanation: First KI + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HI. Then HI reduces the acid: 8HI + H₂SO₄ → 4I₂ + H₂S + 4H₂O. Violet fumes of iodine and the smell of H₂S appear. Sulfur is reduced from +6 to −2, which shows that iodide is a very strong reducing agent, much stronger than bromide (which reduces the acid only to SO₂) and chloride (which does not reduce it at all).

blocks.prompt: b) Show that the reaction of Cl₂ with cold and hot aqueous KOH is a disproportionation reaction.
blocks.explanation:
Cold: Cl₂ + 2KOH → KCl + KClO + H₂O; chlorine goes from 0 to −1 in KCl (reduced) and to +1 in KClO (oxidized).
Hot: 3Cl₂ + 6KOH → 5KCl + KClO₃ + 3H₂O; chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (five atoms) and to +5 (one atom).
In both reactions the same element is both oxidized and reduced, so both are disproportionation reactions.

blocks.prompt: c) HI acts as strong reducing agent. Explain it with chemical reactions.
blocks.explanation: HI reduces concentrated sulfuric acid to H₂S and is itself oxidized to I₂: 8HI + H₂SO₄ → 4I₂ + H₂S + 4H₂O (S: +6 to −2; I: −1 to 0). HBr, by comparison, reduces the acid only to SO₂: 2HBr + H₂SO₄ → Br₂ + SO₂ + 2H₂O (S: +6 to +4). Reducing sulfur much further shows that HI is the stronger reducing agent.
